Virtual Memory and Page Replacement Algorithms Virtual memory decouples the user's logical memory from physical memory, allowing execution of processes whose address spaces exceed available physical RAM. Memory is organized into fixed-size blocks called pages (in logical memory) and frames (in physical memory). When a process attempts to access a page not currently residing in physical RAM, the memory management unit (MMU) generates a page fault hardware interrupt. When a page fault occurs and all memory frames are occupied, a page replacement algorithm must select a victim frame to swap out: - FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Replaces the oldest page loaded in memory. Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly, where increasing the number of page frames results in an increased number of page faults. - Optimal (OPT / Belady's Min): Replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Provides the lowest page fault rate but is impossible to implement in practice because future references cannot be known. - Least Recently Used (LRU): Replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period in the past. Approximates the optimal algorithm by using past temporal locality.

TCP Flow Control vs Congestion Control It is vital to distinguish between flow control and congestion control in computer networks: - Flow Control is a speed-matching service that prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's buffer space. TCP implements flow control using a receive window (`rwnd`) field in the TCP header. The receiver explicitly informs the sender of how many spare bytes of buffer space are currently available (`rwnd = RcvBuffer - [LastByteRcvd - LastByteRead]`). The sender ensures that the unacknowledged data never exceeds `rwnd`. - Congestion Control prevents senders from injecting too much traffic into the network subnet, avoiding packet loss and queue collapse in intermediate routers. TCP maintains a congestion window (`cwnd`). The effective transmission window is $\min(\text{cwnd}, \text{rwnd})$. TCP congestion control algorithms (such as TCP Reno and Tahoe) employ four phases: Slow Start (exponential window growth), Congestion Avoidance (additive increase / multiplicative decrease, AIMD), Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery.

Context-Free Grammars and Pushdown Automata Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) generate the class of context-free languages, which strictly subsume regular languages. A CFG is a 4-tuple (V, Sigma, R, S), where V is a finite set of non-terminal variables, Sigma is the terminal alphabet, R is a finite set of production rules of the form A -> alpha with A in V and alpha in (V union Sigma)*, and S is the start symbol. A Pushdown Automaton (PDA) is the mechanical equivalent of a CFG. It extends a finite state machine with an unbounded Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack storage. Deterministic Pushdown Automata (DPDAs) recognize deterministic context-free languages, which form a strict subset of context-free languages recognized by non-deterministic PDAs (e.g., the language of palindromes {w w^R}).

Algorithms and Data Structures: Graph Traversal and Shortest Paths Dijkstra's Algorithm is a fundamental single-source shortest path algorithm designed for weighted directed or undirected graphs with non-negative edge weights. The algorithm operates by maintaining a set of vertices whose final shortest-path weights from the source have already been determined. At each step, Dijkstra's algorithm greedily selects the vertex with the minimum tentative distance from the priority queue (commonly implemented using a Fibonacci heap or binary min-heap) and relaxes all of its outgoing edges. The relaxation step for an edge (u, v) with weight w(u, v) checks whether the current distance to v satisfies: if dist[v] > dist[u] + w(u, v), then dist[v] is updated to dist[u] + w(u, v). The time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with a binary min-heap is O((V + E) log V), where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges. If implemented with a Fibonacci heap, the running time improves to O(E + V log V).

Operating Systems: Process Synchronization and Deadlocks In multiprogramming environments, concurrent access to shared data can lead to data inconsistency. A race condition arises when several processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently and the outcome depends on the particular order in which access takes place. The critical-section problem requires three structural conditions to be satisfied: 1. Mutual Exclusion: If process P_i is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical sections. 2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and there exist some processes that wish to enter their critical section, then only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter next. 3. Bounded Waiting: There must be a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted.
